## Overview

An end-to-end predictive maintenance pipeline that detects equipment
failure using **unsupervised anomaly detection** on multivariate
sensor data — no labeled failure examples used during training, only
clean "normal operation" data. The project covers the full lifecycle:
raw sensor data → feature engineering → model validation → rigorous
methodology debugging → feature selection experiments → a live
historical-replay dashboard.

**Stack:** Python, scikit-learn (Isolation Forest), pandas, Jupyter,
Plotly/ipywidgets for the live dashboard.

## Problem

Given a stream of ~40 sensor readings from an industrial pump system,
predict impending failure early enough to act on it — using only
examples of *normal* operation, since real failures are rare and
expensive to label. The model needs to generalize across time: trained
on the past, evaluated on the future, the way it would actually be
deployed.

## Approach

- **Isolation Forest**, trained exclusively on clean-baseline
  (normal) operation, flags future readings that don't resemble it.
- **Walk-forward validation** — chronological train/test splits, never
  trained on future data relative to what it's evaluated against.
- **Engineered feature families**: raw sensor readings ("core"),
  rolling mechanical features (velocity, amplitude, accumulated
  stress), and spectral features (FFT energy, dominant frequency,
  spectral entropy) — each tested standalone and in combination.

## Methodology highlights

This project's real emphasis is **rigor over headline numbers** — several
rounds of discovering and correcting subtle methodology issues that
would have otherwise produced misleading results:

- **Found and fixed a feature-selection bias**: an AUC-based ranking
  was unintentionally selecting features that separated
  *post-failure recovery* behavior rather than *failure* behavior
  itself — features with near-perfect individual separation scores
  that produced a near-useless model once combined. Diagnosed by
  breaking AUC down per machine-state pair rather than trusting a
  single combined metric.
- **Found and fixed a feature-scale bug**: an engineered "accumulated
  stress" feature was an unbounded rolling sum, sitting at a scale
  thousands of times larger than other features — silently dominating
  the model's decision splits. Fixed by converting it to a
  scale-normalized rate.
- **Found and fixed a silent pipeline bug**: a per-experiment
  contamination-rate tuning step had been computed but never actually
  wired into model training — every experiment was silently using a
  generic default. Confirmed via a direct before/after comparison
  once corrected.
- **Compared two feature-selection philosophies head-to-head**: ranking
  features by individual statistical separation (AUC) vs. testing each
  feature's actual marginal contribution to model performance
  (ablation). The ablation approach surfaced a real, validated
  precision/recall trade-off that the AUC approach never found.

## Results

The raw sensor readings ("core" features) turned out to be the
strongest standalone predictor — engineered mechanical and spectral
features did **not** reliably improve on this baseline, a genuine
negative result reached only after four separate rounds of fixes and
a second, independent feature-selection method, not an unexamined gap.

| Feature set | F1 | Precision | Recall | Median warning time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Core (raw sensors)** | **0.72** | 0.67 | 0.80 | 978 hrs (~41 days) |
| Ablation-selected (core + engineered) | 0.67 | 0.58 | 0.84 | 1,171 hrs (~49 days) |

The two final candidates represent a genuine trade-off rather than one
being strictly better: the ablation-selected set trades precision and
a higher false-alarm rate for meaningfully earlier warning — about
8 additional days of lead time before failure. Which one is "correct"
depends on the operational cost of a false alarm versus the value of
earlier warning, a business question the model itself can't answer.

## Live demo

![Dashboard Demo](dashboard_v0.gif)

A historical-replay dashboard simulates real-time monitoring by
streaming the historical dataset chronologically through the trained
model — showing live anomaly scores, current machine status, and a
running alert log, since no live sensor feed was available for this
project.

## What's next

Converting the research notebooks into a reproducible `src/` pipeline,
with a streaming inference simulation and basic edge-deployment
resource profiling.
